schemes.description: The Base 3-4 is a staple of modern defense, swapping out a defensive lineman for an extra linebacker in an effort to create confusion for the offense.
The 3-2-6 takes the 3-4's adjustment of swapping a defensive lineman for a linebacker and takes it even further by adding two extra defensive backs to the mix instead.

The 3-3-5 tite looks to plug up the middle of the offense with a large defensive lineman over the Center and the defensive ends "tite" in alignment, with the goal of forcing everything outside to the waiting Linebackers and Defensive Backs.

The 3-3-5 splits the difference between the 3-4 and the 3-2-6, adding back one linebacker in lieu of a defensive back. It involves attacking gaps using the 6-man defensive front with smaller, faster players.
The 3-4 Multiple Defense allows for an additional level of flexibility from the 3-4 alignment.
The 4-2-5 defense features 4 down linemen, 2 Linebackers, and 5 Defensive Backs. The Linebackers and Defensive Backs especially need to be versatile players, able to play the run or pass.
The 4-3 Multiple Defense allows for an additional level of flexibility from the 4-3 alignment.

The 4-3 defensive scheme is consdiered the default for many levels of football. It features 4 defensive linemen and 3 linebackers. The defensive linemen focus on a mix of pass rushing and run stopping, allowing for 7 defenders to drop into coverage.
Multiple Defense teams can do a little bit of everything. Their goal is to find what you do well, and take it away.

An offshoot of the Option, the Spread Option is used by teams that want to mix in plenty of pass along with their run options. Expect many Run/Pass Options (RPOs) and the need for versatile players all over the offense.

The Air Raid is an offshoot of the spread that focuses more on simple concepts run from a variety of formations, allowing the Quarterback to quickly diagnose coverages and find the open receiver, of which there are many.
Multiple Offense teams pick and choose from a variety of offensive styles. Expect to see a little bit of everything.

The Option is the classic collegiate offense that's been used since the days of leather helmets. Although it's fallen out of favor in recent years, the variety of backs running in all different directions combined with a quick Quarterback still trips up defenses if they are not careful.
The Pistol is an adjustment to the traditional Spread that places the running back behind the Quarterback, allowing for more downhill runs compared to the finesse of the shotgun spread.
The Power Spread responds to ever-shrinking defensive personnel by adding additional Tight Ends to the mix, melding the spacing of the Spread Offense with traditional power football run concepts.
The Pro Style Offense replicates what is seen on Sundays. It's more complex than most other schemes, using a wider variety of personnel groupings and formations.

The proliferation of the Spread offense is one of the most important things to happen to the college game. True to its namesake, it "spreads" the defense horizontally and looks for gaps to attack with speedy receivers, backs, and Quarterbacks.

The Veer and Shoot works to spread the defense out with wide alignments with many receivers and few tight ends and backs. It prioritizes a quick pace and creating tough decisions for the defense due to the amount of ground to cover and the speed at which plays are run.
One of the classic collegiate offenses, the Run N' Shoot leans heavily on option routes from Wide Receivers to find holes in the defense and adjust to "run" to space.
